text: The city of waters; that part of the city which supplied the other parts with water; of course the whole must soon surrender.

title: II Samuel 12:31
text:
Under saws; some have supposed the meaning of these words to be, that he put the Ammonites to hard labor with the instruments mentioned. But it is said,  I Chronicles 20:3 , "he cut them with saws, and with harrows of iron, and with axes."  We must then understand that he put them to torture, or more probably to death, with these instruments; a severity which the sacred writer simply records without in any way expressing approbation of it, and which may have been exercised before his repentance in respect to the matter of Uriah. 
 
  Brickkiln; apparently in a burning state.

title: II Samuel 13:1
text: Great beauty, great honor, high station, and much property, are often the occasion of ruin to the possessor.  They should therefore not be coveted.  If bestowed, they should be employed to the honor of God and the good of men; and if not bestowed, we should be contented without them.

title: II Samuel 13:2
text:
Thought it hard; difficult or impracticable. 
 
Were the power of men equal to their wickedness, virtue would be constantly outraged, and earth become an emblem of hell.

title: II Samuel 13:3
text: Wicked men in high stations are ordinarily surrounded by subtle flatters, who labor to secure their favor by tempting them to the commission of sin, and thus become the means of their destruction.

title: II Samuel 13:5
text:
Make; feign, pretend to be. 
 
  Dress the meat; cook him some food, pretending that she could do it better than any one else.   II Samuel 13:6-8

title: II Samuel 13:6
text: No deception is so gross, and no wickedness so horrible, that licentious men in high stations will not practise it with cool deliberation and determined purpose.

title: II Samuel 13:12
text: Natural affection, gratitude, and all kindly feelings, the dictates of conscience, regard to consequences, and every thing which stands in the way of sinful gratification, will be disregarded by those who surrender themselves to its power.

title: II Samuel 13:19
text: There are injuries inflicted which in this world can never be repaired, and distresses which none but God can assuage.  Though he permits such injuries, he does not forget them, nor does he fail in due time to visit their authors with his wrath.   II Samuel 13:29

title: II Samuel 13:21
text:
Was very wroth; but took no measures to inflict punishment upon Amnon for his crime.  This leniency seems to have proceeded partly from parental fondness, and partly from the recollection of his own heinous crime. 
 
It is not enough for rulers to be angry at the foul crimes of their subjects; they should punish them, that others may fear and be restrained from practising such iniquities.  Nor, while they remember with shame their own sins, and the injurious influence they may have exerted on others, should they let natural affection or a sense of their own guilt hinder them from doing their duty.   Romans 13:3-4

title: II Samuel 13:24
text: Sheep-shearers; at sheep-shearing it was customary to make a feast and invite friends.

title: II Samuel 13:28
text: When rulers, whose office it is to punish crime, neglect their duty, the natural result is the commission of further crimes.

title: II Samuel 13:29
text: One wicked man, in the indulgence of his hateful passions, may be the instrument of executing not only his own wrath, but the just indignation of God against another, and then in due time be himself punished, and that for ever and ever.   II Samuel 17:14 II Samuel 17:23 I Kings 2:31-34

title: II Samuel 13:37
text: Talmai; Absalom's grandfather.   II Samuel 3:3

title: II Samuel 13:39
text: Comforted concerning Amnon; was less grieved at his death, than at the absence of Absalom.

title: II Samuel 14:1
text:
The king's heart was toward Absalom; he wished for some pretext to bring him back. 
 
Courtiers, and those who covet royal favor, are quick to discern the inclinations of rulers, and skillful in devising means and presenting inducements to gratify them.

title: II Samuel 14:2
text:
Tekoah; in Judah, a few miles south-east of Bethlehem. 
 
When great men and those in authority are set upon accomplishing their selfish objects, they will generally find agents deceitful and wicked enough to aid them.

title: II Samuel 14:4
text: Flatterers and those who are engaged in artful projects, are often most complaisant and respectful to those whose favor they seek, and whom they are aiming to deceive.

title: II Samuel 14:5
text: Compassion towards the distressed and desires to grant relief should be regulated by correct knowledge and sound judgment.

title: II Samuel 14:7
text: Quench my coal; destroy her son.

title: II Samuel 14:8
text:
Give charge concerning thee; directions that she should not be injured. 
 
It is ordinarily unwise to decide a case on the testimony of one party, especially one that is interested and likely to be strongly biassed in his own favor.

title: II Samuel 14:9
text: Iniquity be on me; the blame, if there was any, of his deciding that her son should not be slain.

title: II Samuel 14:12
text: Speak one word; having got David to decide that her son, who she said had killed his brother, should not be hurt, she wished now to make the application to Ablalom, sho had killed Amnon.

title: II Samuel 14:13
text:
Such a thing; more literally, a thing like this; that is, like what my family proposed to do in the case of my son. 
 
  Against the people of God; implying that David was injuring them by keeping Absalom in banishment, and having decided that her son should be spared, was faulty in not sparing his own son, and bringing him back from banishment. 
 
After persons are committed on the wrong side, those who are interested will endeavor to take advantage of that commitment to lead them still further into error and transgression.

title: II Samuel 14:14
text:
Yet doth he devise means; as God devises means to save men, and is ready to be reconciled to them, her implication was that David should be reconciled to Absalom. 
 
Those who so sympathize with murderers as to try to screen them from the punishment which God has directed, often refer to his mercy as a reason why his directions should not be followed; as if his justice were at war with his mercy, or as if they were more merciful than God.

title: II Samuel 14:15
text:
The people have made me afraid; as she stated,  II Samuel 14:7  and she insinuated that there would be greater reason to fear the people, if Absalom should not be brought back, as they greatly desired it. 
 
  I will now speak unto the king; state a case as if it were her own, and then apply it to Absalom.

title: II Samuel 14:17
text: As an angel of God; wise and discerning.

title: II Samuel 14:20
text: To fetch about this form of speech; or, to change the face of this matter; that is, to give a new turn to the matter of Absalom's banishment.

title: II Samuel 14:21
text:
I have done this thing; he had decided, in the supposed case, that the woman's son should not be hurt, and was ready to make the desired application to Absalom. 
 
When rulers, through fear or favor, natural affection, or improper sympathy, fail to punish murderers, or pardon and receive them into favor, they take a course which tends to increase crime, and to bring upon themselves and others great distresses.

title: II Samuel 14:22
text: Grace; favor.

title: II Samuel 14:25
text: Men are prone to regard and be greatly influenced by mere external accomplishments, while the most beautiful form and graceful exterior may cover a polluted and murderous heart.

title: II Samuel 14:26
text: After the king's weight; some have thought this to be much less than the common shekel.

title: II Samuel 14:30
text: Connivance at crime, or an utterly inadequate punishment, tends to increase haughtiness, pride, and self-will in criminals, and to lead them on from one crime to another till they perish.

title: II Samuel 14:33
text: Parents who only kiss their children when they should punish them, have reason to fear that God, in righteous judgment, will suffer their children by their wickedness to become instruments of punishing their parents.   II Samuel 16:11 II Samuel 16:21 II Samuel 16:22 II Samuel 18:9 II Samuel 18:14 II Samuel 18:33

title: II Samuel 15:1
text: Men of weak minds and depraved hearts are peculiarly fond of personal decoration and external display, while the truly worthy and noble seek principally internal excellence and those spiritual ornaments which alone are, in the sight of the Lord, of great price.

title: II Samuel 15:2
text: The way of the gate; where the people assembled for judgment, or to obtain the king's decision of their cases.

title: II Samuel 15:3
text:
No man deputed of the king; he spoke as if David was negligent of his duty in not appointing him or some one to hear them. 
 
Familiarity and flattery, high promises of gratification, and strong expressions of regard for the people, mark the efforts of heartless demagogues to delude the multitude and promote their own elevation to office.

title: II Samuel 15:5
text: Many a good cause has been betrayed, and many a bad one promoted, by a kiss.   Luke 22:48

title: II Samuel 15:6
text: Stole the hearts; led the people to admire him.

title: II Samuel 15:7
text: Where godliness is respected, the most villanous conduct is sometimes masked under the semblance of piety, and those most pleased with the appearance of religion may be most readily deceived.   Jeremiah 17:9

title: II Samuel 15:9
text: Go in peace; he probably hoped that Absalom was becoming better.

title: II Samuel 15:11
text: Called; invited to go with Absalom, supposing his object was, as he stated, a religious one.

title: II Samuel 15:12
text:
Ahithophel; he had been a great friend to David, but now deserted him.   II Samuel 17:23  
 
  Giloh; in the mountainous parts of Judah.   Joshua 15:51  
 
Traitors and apostates are among the most virulent enemies, and those whom we have especially favored, and treated with confidence, may become our bitterest foes.   Psalms 41:9 Psalms 55:12-14

title: II Samuel 15:13
text: No one, however exalted or meritorious, can safely depend on popular favor.  At one time the people may eulogize, and at another curse him; at one time cry, Hosanna, and at another crucify him.  Matthew 21:9 Mark 7:37 Luke 7:34 Luke 23:21

title: II Samuel 15:19
text:
Ittai; the commander of the Gittites. 
 
  The king; Absalom, who had proclaimed himself king. 
 
  Thou art a stranger; the Gittites were from the Philistines, but had become attached to David and his cause. 
 
A generous and benevolent mind will not wish its friends to be involved in its troubles, but will desire, as far as may be consistent, to relieve them, and to promote their enjoyment.

title: II Samuel 15:21
text: True love is gratified not only in labors, but in self-denials and sacrifices to relieve the distresses and advance the happiness of the object beloved.

title: II Samuel 15:23
text: The brook Kidron; on the east side of Jerusalem, between the city and the mount of Olives.

title: II Samuel 15:24
text: Abiathar; he was high-priest at that time.

title: II Samuel 15:25
text: Humble and hearty submission in distress to the chastising hand of God, and cheerful commitment of one's interests to him, form a good preparation for deliverance.

title: II Samuel 15:27
text: A seer; a prophet, or a wise and discerning man.

title: II Samuel 15:30
text:
His head covered; in token of deep humiliation and distress.  He was reaping the fruit of kissing Absalom when he should have punished him, and also the fruit of his own sins in the matter of Uriah.  II Samuel 14:33 II Samuel 11:2-27  
 
Parents for their sins are often chastised by the sins of children, which are the occasion to them and their friends of many tears.

title: II Samuel 15:31
text:
Turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness; by preventing it from helping Absalom or injuring David. 
 
A very short but hearty supplication to God may be answered in great and lasting blessings.   II Samuel 17:23 Genesis 17:18 Luke 23:34 John 17:24

title: II Samuel 15:36
text: Prayer, though effcacious, does not lessen the necessity of using means; and in cases of difficulty, the more knowledge a person has with regard to them, the more properly he will be able to treat them.  But no means should be used to gain knowledge, or accomplish any object, but such as are right, and no declarations made except those which are true.   Proverbs 12:17 Proverbs 12:19 Proverbs 12:20 Proverbs 12:22

title: II Samuel 16:1
text:
The hill; Olivet.   II Samuel 15:30  
 
  Ziba;  II Samuel 9:2 II Samuel 9:9-13:1 2Sa 9.2,9-13. 
 
  A bottle; bottles then were whole skins of animals, and some held a large quantity.

title: II Samuel 16:2
text: Sympathy and kindness under trials deeply affect the generous heart, and sometimes the pretence of them is used to conceal the basest selfishness.

title: II Samuel 16:3
text:
Thy master's son; Mephibosheth.   II Samuel 9:6-13  
 
  Ziba said; what was not true, but was a slander on Mephibosheth, for the purpose of getting his estate.   II Samuel 19:26-27

title: II Samuel 16:4
text:
Thine are all; a hasty and unjust decision of David. 
 
Hasty decisions under the influence of strongly excited feelings, without taking time for deliberation, or asking direction of God, are generally wrong and often are exceedingly unjust and cruel.

title: II Samuel 16:5
text:
Bahurim; a city in the tribe of Benjamin. 
 
  Shimei; a relative of Saul.

title: II Samuel 16:7
text:
Come out; in the original, Go out; flee from the kingdom, as not fit to live in it. 
 
A malignant heart rejoices in the calamities of those it hates, and is gratified in tormenting them.

title: II Samuel 16:10
text:
The Lord hath said; so ordered things in his providence, that this, as well as other trials, should come upon David as a punishment for his sins. 
 
A penitent soul will never overlook the hand of God in its trials, whoever and whatever may be the instruments of them; and when we heartily submit to his corrections, without any wrong feelings towards the instruments of them, they will in the end promote our good.

title: II Samuel 16:11
text: My son--seeketh my life; David wickedly sought the life of Uriah, and now Absalom wickedly sought his, and Shimei wickedly cursed him.

title: II Samuel 16:16
text:
Hushai;  II Samuel 15:1 
  God save the king; he did not say which king he wished God to save, whether Absalom or David, though he meant that Absalom should understand it of himself. 
 
Men who undertake to deceive others are strongly tempted to use language which is equivocal, and may be understood as meaning one thing or another according to the situation of different parties, and which, in the sense in which they design to be understood, is positively false.

title: II Samuel 16:17
text: Thy friend; David.

title: II Samuel 16:21
text:
Thy father's concubines;  II Samuel 15:1 
  Abhorred of thy father; for his wickedness, so that his father would not again be reconciled to him. 
 
The wickedness of the wicked is made instrumental by God in correcting and sanctifying his people, and thus in fulfilling his declarations of judgment and mercy concerning them.   II Samuel 12:11-12 Acts 2:23

title: II Samuel 17:1
text:
Pursue after David this night; with the intent of killing him.  He understood that the success of the conspiracy depended on a decisive stroke at the beginning, and that the death of David could alone make the throne sure to Absalom. 
 
Apostates and traitors who give themselves up to iniquity, are often left to go from one degree of sin to another till they plunge into irretrievable ruin.

title: II Samuel 17:4
text: If parents do not govern their children and effectually subdue them when young, they will be in danger afterwards of being subdued by them.

title: II Samuel 17:7
text: That counsel which would be most likely to succeed, should it be followed, may still not be good.  It may spring from evil, tend to evil, and its prosecution be productive of mischief; still, no one has a right to do evil in order to defeat it.

title: II Samuel 17:11
text: That all Israel be--gathered; Hushai proposed this magnificent but foolish plan, which flattered the vanity of Absalom, to gain time for David, and prevent the execution of Ahithophel's purpose.

title: II Samuel 17:14
text:
The Lord had appointed; he so ordered events that Absalom should prefer the counsel of Hushai to that of Ahithophel, and thus penitent, believing David be saved, and impenitent, unbelieving Absalom be destroyed. 
 
The Lord can easily defeat the craftiest counsels, disappoint the best-concerted schemes, and overrule all things for the salvation of his friends and the destruction of his enemies.

title: II Samuel 17:16
text:
Pass over; over the river Jordan.   II Samuel 17:22  
 
Men must make efforts to save themselves with as much promptness, skill, energy, and perseverance, as if their slavation depended solely on their efforts; while it is God who renders those efforts successful, and to him, if they feel right, they will give the glory.

title: II Samuel 17:17
text: En-rogel; on the south-east side of Jerusalem.

title: II Samuel 17:23
text:
Put his household in order; settled up his affairs. 
 
  Hanged himself; he understood that Absalom's cause was lost, and with it all his own hopes. 
 
The way of transgressors is hard, and the wages of sin is death; when men are given up to its power, it makes them wretched here and plunges them into endless wretchedness hereafter.

title: II Samuel 17:24
text: Mahanaim;  II Samuel 2:1

title: II Samuel 17:25
text: Amasa; he and Joab were cousins, and were sons of David's sisters.

title: II Samuel 17:27
text: Lo-debar--Rogelim; in the tribe of Gad, not far from Mahanaim.

title: II Samuel 18:3
text:
Succor us out of the city; by sending them what they might need. 
 
All should consider in what way they can be most useful, and be disposed to take that course in which they can do the greatest good.

title: II Samuel 18:5
text: The love of parents to their children is ordinarily much greater than that of children to their parents.  Sometimes it overcomes their judgment, and leads them to act in such a manner as is exceedingly injurious to themselves, their children, and the community.

title: II Samuel 18:6
text: The wood of Ephraim; on the east side of Jordan.

title: II Samuel 18:8
text: The wood devoured; more perished in their flight through the woods, than had been slain in the open field.

title: II Samuel 18:9
text: Though criminals may sometimes escape from their fellow men, they cannot escape from God.  However great their efforts, his judgment will in due time overtake and destroy them.

title: II Samuel 18:12
text: Though money is valuable and has great influence with men, yet it is foolish to endanger one's life for it, and much more foolish to endanger one's soul.

title: II Samuel 18:13
text: Wrought falsehood; acted in such a manner as to endanger his own life.

title: II Samuel 18:14
text: One criminal is often made the means of punishing another, and he may do it for an object and with a spirit which may justly draw down punishment on himself.

title: II Samuel 18:17
text: Children who rebel against and ill treat their parents, are in special dnager of coming to an untimely and miserable end.

title: II Samuel 18:18
text: The king's dale; near Jerusalem.   Genesis 14:17-18

title: II Samuel 18:20
text: The immediate effect of joyful or mournful tidings depends much on the manner in which they are communicated.  Care should therefore be taken to have it done by such persons and in such a manner as will tend to produce the best results.

title: II Samuel 18:24
text:
Between the two gates; of the city Mahanaim.   I Samuel 17:24  
 
  The roof; of the watchhouse.

title: II Samuel 18:27
text: Our wished have a great influence on our judgment, and high expectations of good are liable to be followed by distressing accumulations of evil.

title: II Samuel 18:29
text: I knew not what it was; not having been entrusted by Joab with the message concerning Absalom's death, he does not venture to communicate it, though he was fully aware of it,  II Samuel 18:20 .

title: II Samuel 18:32
text: The enemies of my lord--be as that young man is; implying that he was dead.

title: II Samuel 18:33
text:
Died for thee; instead of thee, in thy place. 
 
None fully know the sufferings of affectionate parents in the untimely and violent death of children, but those who endure them; and none but those who experience it can imagine the blessedness, at such times, of intelligent, affectionate, childlike confidence in God, and a hearty commitment of all one's interests to his infinitely wise and good disposal.

title: II Samuel 19:2
text: Excessive sorrow unfits the soul for duty, displeases God, and tends to injure all who indulge it or feel its influence.

title: II Samuel 19:3
text: Gat them by stealth; secretly, privately, because the king appeared as if he was displeased at what they had done.

title: II Samuel 19:6
text:
Thou lovest thine enemies; Joab's meaning was, that David by so mourning for Absalom acted as if he loved him more than he did his family and people, whose lives had been saved by the death of Absalom. 
 
Rulers, as well as people, should be plainly told of their duty, and such motives set before them as are suited to induce them to perform it.

title: II Samuel 19:7
text: Speak comfortably unto thy servants; show thyself pleased with their victory.

title: II Samuel 19:8
text: The approbation of rulers should be promptly and cheerfully given to those who do right, and their disapprobation manifested towards those who do wrong.   Romans 13:3-4

title: II Samuel 19:11
text:
The speech of all Israel is come; expressing their desire to have the king return. 
 
All prudent care should be taken to avoid coming evils, especially to prevent discord among brethren, and to lead them to cooperate for the public good.

title: II Samuel 19:12
text: My flesh; of the same tribe with him.

title: II Samuel 19:13
text:
Amasa; he had been the commander of Absalom's army.   II Samuel 17:25  
 
When men are strongly excited and set upon accomplishing a favorite object, they are tempted to make rash promises, and to adopt measures which events show to have been unwise.

title: II Samuel 19:14
text: He bowed the heart of all the men of Judah; according to some, Amasa did this; but others understand David as doing it through his messages to Zadok and Abiathar.

title: II Samuel 19:19
text:
Thy servant did perversely;   
 
If men confess their sins and appear to be penitent, it is ordinarily wise to treat them as if they were so.  God alone knows the heart, and men ought not to judge of it, except so far as its character is manifested in the conduct.

title: II Samuel 19:23
text: Not die; not be put to death for that offence.

title: II Samuel 19:24
text:
Neither dressed--nor trimmed--nor washed; showing that he had been in a state of deep mourning ever since David left the city. 
 
True love will show itself in grief at the sorrows of those beloved, and in joy at the return of their joys.

title: II Samuel 19:26
text: My servant; Ziba.

title: II Samuel 19:27
text:
Slandered thy servant;   
 
Slander is a common and aggravated sin, and the slanderer, though he often escape punishment from men, is and ought to be regarded as among the basest of sinners.

title: II Samuel 19:29
text: Divide the land; the land that had belonged to Saul, and which David, after restoring it to Mephibosheth, had hastily given to Ziba.  II Samuel 9:7 II Samuel 16:4

title: II Samuel 19:31
text: Barzillai;  II Samuel 17:1

title: II Samuel 19:32
text: Kindness and active benevolence are peculiarly agreeable in the aged, and should ever be met with grateful and active kindness in return.  As their tastes for the comforts of this life are diminishing, their desires for those of the future should be increasing, and their chief concern be for preparation to close their work on earth, and enter the rest of heaven.

title: II Samuel 19:37
text:
Chimham; he seems to have been the son of Barzillai.   I Kings 2:7  
 
Aged benevolent men are pleased to have those who are younger partake of lawful innocent enjoyments, for which they themselves have no relish.

title: II Samuel 19:38
text: The kindness and fidelity of parents the Lord often rewards in blessings on their children and children's children; thus showing mercy even to thousands of those who love him and keep his commandments.

title: II Samuel 19:41
text: Stolen thee away; gone first and brought the king without consulting the other tribes.   II Samuel 19:43

title: II Samuel 19:42
text: Near of kin; he belonged to their tribe.

title: II Samuel 20:1
text: Many difficulties might be amicably settled, did not some wicked man take occasion to fan the flame, and lead on to acts of rashness destructive, it may be, to himself and to his fellow men.

title: II Samuel 20:3
text: In ward; in seclusion.

title: II Samuel 20:6
text: Abishai; Joab may not have been at that moment present in Jerusalem, so that the charge was given to Abishai.  But we find Joab with Abishai soon after,  II Samuel 20:8 .

title: II Samuel 20:8
text:
Amasa went before them; or, came before them, met them on his return from assembling the men of Judah. 
 
  It fell out; it is probable that Joab so managed as to have the sword fall out as he approached Amasa.  However this may be, it is plain that he took it up with his left hand, while he extended his right hand to take Amasa by the beard.

title: II Samuel 20:10
text:
He smote him; as he had before smitten Abner,  II Samuel 3:27 ; being angry because David had put Amasa over him. 
 
Many a bold and successful warrior has the heart of an assassin, and will without scruple murder even his own relatives who stand in the way of his advancement.   II Samuel 3:27 II Samuel 4:6

title: II Samuel 20:12
text: Stood still; to gaze, and were thus hindered from going forward to Joab and Abishai.

title: II Samuel 20:14
text: Abel and--Beth-maachah; called also Abel of Beth-maachah, to distinguish it from several other places that bore the name of Abel. It was on the east of the Jordan, at the foot of Anti-Lebanon.

title: II Samuel 20:15
text:
It stood in the trench; or, he (Joab) stood on the outer wall this was a low wall with a trench, encompassing the inner wall. 
 
The presence of none man may endanger the destruction of a whole city, and the wisdom of one woman may do more than all its men of war towards saving it.

title: II Samuel 20:18
text:
To speak; in proverbs. 
 
  Ask counsel at Abel; as a place celebrated for wisdom. 
 
  And so; by listening to the counsel of its wise men. 
 
  They ended the matter; brought it to a successful termination. Joab ought not therefore to destroy such a city without a hearing.

title: II Samuel 20:19
text: A mother in Israel; one of its chief cities.

title: II Samuel 20:22
text: Magistrates, by putting to death one criminal, may save the lives of many who are innocent.

title: II Samuel 21:1
text: Temporal calamities are the consequences of sin, and should lead those who suffer them to self-examination, repentance, and reformation.

title: II Samuel 21:2
text: In his zeal to the children of Israel and Judah; he would have destroyed them, not for any wrong act on their part, but simply because they were remnants of the Canaanites, in direct violation of the oath of Joshua and the elders of Israel,   Joshua 9:15-27 .  The sin was therefore one of the nation whom Saul represented, and God punished it by a national calamity.

title: II Samuel 21:3
text: Bless the inheritance; that the famine might cease, and the Israelites have the blessings of harvests.

title: II Samuel 21:6
text: The wickedness of parents may bring great calamities on their children, and the wickedness of rulers great calamities on their people, long after such parents and rulers are dead.  Though the Lord delays, he does not forget, and in due time will manifest his just indignation against sin.

title: II Samuel 21:7
text: The Lord's oath;

title: II Samuel 21:8
text: Michal; it was Merab, the sister of Michal, who married Adriel the Meholathite,  I Samuel 18:19 .  Some suppose they are here called Michal's sons because she had the education of them.

title: II Samuel 21:9
text: Barley-harvest; in March.

title: II Samuel 21:10
text:
Water dropped upon them; the rain was a token of God's reconciliation.  If it fell at the usual time, it was about the middle of October. 
 
The condition of children is often a source of great distress to parents, and occasions them troubles under which none but God can comfort, and from which none else can relieve them.

title: II Samuel 21:12
text: The bones of Saul;

title: II Samuel 21:14
text:
Was entreated for the land; removed the famine by sending rain. 
 
The common blessings of life all come from God, and every new harvest lays men under new obligations to love and obey him.

title: II Samuel 21:17
text:
Quench not the light; not deprive the nation of the blessings of David's reign. 
 
The life, health, and reputation of good rulers are great blessings to the people, for the possession and continuance of which they should earnestly pray, and, when granted, be especially grateful.

title: II Samuel 21:19
text: Great bodily strength and vigor are apt to be idolized, and when they are, often prove occasions of ruin to their possessors.

title: II Samuel 22:1
text: Deliverance from trouble should be ever followed by devout acknowledgment of God as its author, and hearty thanksgiving for his mercies.

title: II Samuel 22:2
text: Rock, and--fortress; support and protection.

title: II Samuel 22:3
text:
The God of my rock;  II Samuel 22:47 II Corinthians 1:1 
  Shield; defence from enemies. 
 
  Horn; the emblem of power. 
 
  Tower; source of security.

title: II Samuel 22:4
text: Humble dependence on God with believing supplication to him for all which is needed, is one of the best means of gaining benefit from trials while they last, and in due time a glorious deliverance from them.

title: II Samuel 22:5
text:
Waves of death; calamities breaking in upon him like the waves of the sea, and threatening to destroy him. 
 
  Floods of ungodly men; this figure expresses both their multitude and their impetuous force.

title: II Samuel 22:6
text: Prevented; this word originally meant, to go before, so as to stop one's way.

title: II Samuel 22:8
text:
vv 8-16. 
 
A highly poetical description of God's appearing for the deliverance of his servant, and the destruction of his enemies. 
 
All created things are dependent upon and under the control of Jehovah, and whenever he sees best he can use them as instruments for the salvation of his friends and the destruction of his enemies.

title: II Samuel 22:13
text: Through the brightness--kindled; or, from the brightness that was before him burning coals proceeded.

title: II Samuel 22:16
text: Channels--appeared, the foundations of the world were discovered; the waters are represented as fleeing at God's presence, so that the deep channels of the sea are laid bare to human vision.

title: II Samuel 22:17
text: Many waters; great afflictions.  See note to  II Samuel 22:5

title: II Samuel 22:19
text: Prevented; see note to  II Samuel 22:6 .

title: II Samuel 22:20
text: Into a large place; where I had freedom from my enemies and the distresses they brought upon me.  The figure is taken from military life, where nothing is so dangerous as to be hemmed in among narrow defiles.

title: II Samuel 22:21
text:
Righteousness--cleanness of my hands; his innocence of the sins charged upon him, and his hearty devotion to the service of God. 
 
The Lord often treats men in this world according to their character; and he will always do it in the world to come.

title: II Samuel 22:24
text:
Upright; honest, sincere, and merciful. 
 
  Mine iniquity; that to which he was most tempted.

title: II Samuel 22:27
text: Show thyself unsavory; he would contend with, oppose, and punish them.

title: II Samuel 22:28
text: The humble, sincere, and benevolent are objects of God's favor, and receive special tokens of his love; while the proud, hypocritical, and selfish he abhors, and will visit with his displeasure.

title: II Samuel 22:29
text: My lamp; showing him the way in which he should go.

title: II Samuel 22:30
text:
Run through; broken. 
 
  Leaped over a wall; scaled the wall of the enemy.

title: II Samuel 22:34
text:
Like hinds' feet; very swift, and able to stand in safety on the most dangerous places. 
 
There are no difficulties in the path of duty which those who trust in God may not overcome, and no dangers which they may not escape.

title: II Samuel 22:35
text: A bow of steel is broken; or, according to some translators, is bent; showing that God had given him great strength.

title: II Samuel 22:36
text: Gentleness; condescending kindness and teaching.

title: II Samuel 22:37
text: Enlarged my steps; given me full liberty and enabled me to walk in safety.

title: II Samuel 22:40
text: God adapts his dealings to the circumstances of his people, and gives mercies according to their necessities; so that as their day is, their wisdom, strength, consolation, and all needful blessings will be.  Deuteronomy 33:25

title: II Samuel 22:41
text: The necks of mine enemies; the meaning of the original is, Thou hast caused mine enemies to turn their backs before me.

title: II Samuel 22:42
text: Answered them not; their cry to him was that of distress merely, after they were given up to ruin as a punishment for their sins.  Proverbs 1:28

title: II Samuel 22:45
text: From what God has done for his people they are encouraged as to what he will do, and led confidently to expect that he will fulfil his promises for ever.

title: II Samuel 22:46
text: Shall be afraid out of their close places; shall come forth out of them with fear.

title: II Samuel 23:1
text:
The last words of David; the last that he spoke under the immediate inspiration of God's Spirit; or the last inspired song that he dictated.  Perhaps, also, they are literally his last words, for it seems probable that the events recorded in this and the following chapter are not given in the exact order of time.  Those recorded in the first book of Kings are from the pen of another author. 
 
The last words of good men often make a deep impression on survivors, and their past labors, directed and aided by the Spirit of God, may to the end of time assist others in preparing for heaven.

title: II Samuel 23:2
text: As the Spirit of God spoke by David, the words which under His guidance he uttered were the words of God; and Peter, in declaring that the Holy Ghost spoke by the mouth of David, uttered nothing but what was true.  Acts 1:16

title: II Samuel 23:3
text: Parents, masters, magistrates, and rulers of every description, are under sacred obligations to be in all things strictly just; they are forbidden by Jehovah to exercise the least injustice towards any whom they govern.

title: II Samuel 23:4
text: Rulers who obey God and so rule as to please him, are great blessings to themselves, their families, and the world.

title: II Samuel 23:5
text:
Although my house be not so with God; though my family be not in many respects such in character as the just ruler whom I have described. 
 
  Although he make it not to grow; although my family do not increase in piety and prosperity as I could desire.  But some prefer to render these two clauses interrogatively, thus: "Is not my house so with God?" and, "Shall he not make it to grow?"  That is, Shall he not establish my house for ever, according to the everlasting covenant he has made with me?  The promise that David's house should be established for ever is fulfilled in Christ, the son of David.  See note to 2Sa 7.12. And it is in Christ alone that the idea of a perfect ruler, such as David here describes, is realized.  Compare the very similar language used of Christ's reign,  Psalms 72:6-7 Psalms 72:12-14 . 
 
Parents, however exalted, cannot with certainty secure the piety of their children, nor masters of their servants, nor rulers of their people; and even for their own piety and salvation they are dependent upon the rich grace of God in Jesus Christ.  The everlasting covenant made with him and his people is their only security.  In this they delight, and the salvation it proffers they supremely desire.

title: II Samuel 23:6
text:
Thorns thrust away; rejected as worthless, and destined to be rooted out and burned. 
 
  Cannot be taken with hands; that is, cannot be plucked away with unarmed hands. 
 
Though the wicked may here for a time prosper, and the righteous be in trouble, yet their condition will soon be reversed; the righteous through grace will be comforted, and the wicked through their persevering wickedness will be tormented.   Malachi 3:18 Luke 16:25

title: II Samuel 23:7
text: Shall touch them; take hold of them to destroy them.  Among the sons of Belial David probably included such men as Joab, whom he found himself unable to root out during his own reign.  See  I Kings 2:5 .

title: II Samuel 23:8
text:
The Tachmonite--chief among the captains; compare  I Chronicles 11:11 , where the number slain by him is stated at three hundred.  In very brief notices like this, apparent discrepancies frequently occur, which a more minute statement of circumstances might remove.  Some, however, suppose that an error of number has been admitted in transcribing. 
 
Different men have different talents, both in kind and degree; but all their capacities and powers they receive from God, and should employ in learning and doing his will.  They will thus best secure their own welfare, and do the most good of which they are capable to others.

title: II Samuel 23:11
text: Lentiles; a species of pulse or pea.

title: II Samuel 23:13
text:
Adullam;  I Samuel 22:1 
  Rephaim;  II Samuel 5:1 
 
vv 13-17. 
 
We should ever be ready to deny ourselves and endure privation, rather than jeopard the lives or injure the souls of our fellow men.  I Corinthians 8:9-13

title: II Samuel 23:17
text: The blood of the men; water for which they had hazarded their lives.

title: II Samuel 23:20
text:
Kabzeel; in the south part of Judah.   Joshua 15:21  
 
  Lion-like; fierce, strong, courageous.

title: II Samuel 23:21
text: A goodly man; one of warlike appearance, and of great strength and stature.   I Chronicles 11:23

title: II Samuel 24:1
text:
Kindled against Israel; on account of their sins. 
 
  He moved David against them; David was moved or tempted by Satan to commit a sin, which was made instrumental in punishing the Israelites for their sins.   I Chronicles 21:1 James 1:13-14  
 
Rulers are often left to act very foolishly and wickedly, and Satan is suffered to tempt them to the commission of sins, which occasion dreadful calamities as a punishment for the sin of the people.

title: II Samuel 24:2
text:
Go now through all the tribes of Israel, and number ye the people; he had no good reason for this act, which seems to have been prompted by a feeling of pride and ambitious curiosity. 
 
A rapid increase of population and great prosperity among a people may make not only them but their rulers proud, overbearing, and self-confident, and may thus draw down upon them the sore and desolating judgments of heaven.

title: II Samuel 24:3
text: Even wicked men see with great clearness that the course which Christians sometimes are disposed to take is morally wrong, and will end in trouble.  They sometimes give warning and advice which it would be well for Christians to follow.

title: II Samuel 24:4
text: Despotic power tends to blind the mind and harden the heart.  Those who possess it are often deaf to reason, and bent on a course which will bring great troubles on themselves and others.

title: II Samuel 24:5
text: Aroer; a city in the south-east part of the country.

title: II Samuel 24:6
text:
Gilead--Tahtim-hadshi--Dan-jaan; places between Aroer and the north border of Canaan. 
 
  Zidon; at the north-west corner.

title: II Samuel 24:7
text:
Tyre; south of Zidon. 
 
  Beer-sheba; the southern extremity of the country.

title: II Samuel 24:10
text: A good man's conscience, though it sometimes in his commission of sin seems to be dead, is nevertheless alive; and it will sooner or later awake, condemn him for his iniquity, fill him with pungent grief, and deep, heart-felt contrition, and lead him to most earnest supplications to God for mercy.

title: II Samuel 24:11
text: David's seer; a prophet who made known to him the will of God.

title: II Samuel 24:12
text: No degree of penitence or faith in Jesus Christ will save the guilty in this world from many of the distressing effects of their sins, nor can they be sure that they will not be the occasion of bringing upon others endless destruction.

title: II Samuel 24:14
text:
Into the hand of the Lord; this he chose the pestilence, which came as an immediate infliction from God. 
 
The only resource for the truly penitent is in hearty submission to God, and unreserved commitment of all their interests to him.

title: II Samuel 24:16
text:
Repented him; changed his course of conduct. 
 
  Araunah the Jebusite; the Jebusites were the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the Araunah's threshing-floor was probably on the site of the future temple.   I Chronicles 22:1  
 
Jehovah is a God of infinite compassion.  He has no pleasure in the ruin even of the most guilty, and punishes as few and as little as will possibly consist with the highest public good.  In the turning of sinners from the error of their ways, he has great delight.

title: II Samuel 24:17
text:
These sheep; the Israelites. 
 
Few things are more distressing to a truly ingenuous and benevolent mind, than to have been the guilty occasion of bringing distress upon others, and it often wishes that the consequences of its own sins could be borne only by itself.

title: II Samuel 24:24
text: Fifty shekels of silver; he further paid him six hundred shekels of gold for "the place of the threshing-floor."   I Chronicles 21:22-25

title: II Samuel 24:25
text: There is no effectual and permanent relief from the sufferings which sin occasions, or from sin itself, but in hearty application, according to the directions of God, to Him who died the just for the unjust, offering himself a sacrifice for sin, and thus obtaining eternal redemption for all who put their trust in him.

title: I Kings 1:1
text: If life is spared, age and infirmities will come, and no means or efforts of men can save any one from death.  All should therefore make it their great object so to live that death shall be gain.

title: I Kings 1:5
text: Haggith; one of David's wives.

title: I Kings 1:6
text:
Bare him after; he was next in age to Absalom, whose mother's name was Maacah.   II Samuel 3:3-4  
 
Over-indulgent parents are often cursed with rebellious children; and inordinate desires for political distinctions have involved multitudes in ruin.

title: I Kings 1:8
text: Shimei; supposed to have been Shimei the son of Elah, afterwards one of Solomon's officers.   I Kings 4:18

title: I Kings 1:9
text:
En-rogel; a fountain on the south-east of Jerusalem, in the valley of Kedron. 
 
Feastings and carousals have strong attractions for the thoughtless, and are often used to draw them into dissipation and crime.

title: I Kings 1:12
text:
Save thine own life, and the life of thy son; had Adonijah succeeded, it would have been his policy to put Solomon, and probably his mother also, to death; as the people knew that David intended that he should be his successor, and there would have been a strong party in his favor.   I Kings 1:21  
 
All wise and proper means should be used to prevent the success of evil projects, and aid those which will honor God and benefit men.

title: I Kings 1:21
text:
I and my son Solomon shall be counted offenders; we shall be regarded and treated as persons deserving to die. 
 
Parents should do what is practicable to prevent evils from coming on their families after their death, and to secure for them permanent blessings.

title: I Kings 1:27
text: Good rulers, who have secured general confidence, may by their dying advice greatly promote the welfare of their people.

title: I Kings 1:32
text: What is essential for the public good should not be postponed, lest the opportunity of doing it be lost; but should be undertaken with promptness, and prosecuted with energy till it is accomplished.

title: I Kings 1:33
text: Gihon; a fountain on the west side of Jerusalem.

title: I Kings 1:37
text: When God is duly acknowledged as the author of all good, men may reasonably expect that their blessings will be increased.

title: I Kings 1:49
text: The most sanguine projects of the wicked are destined to disappointment; and from the heights of expectation they may suddenly be thrown into the depths of despair.

title: I Kings 1:50
text: Horns of the altar; as a sacred place, where it was not customary to put criminals to death.  The wilful murderer was to be taken from the altar before he was slain.   Exodus 21:14

title: I Kings 1:52
text: Will show himself a worthy man--if wickedness shall be found in him; Solomon will pass by for the present Adonijah's offence, and put him upon his good behavior.

title: I Kings 2:3
text: To walk in the way of the Lord by keeping his commandments is, in rulers as well as people, not only right and honorable, but the surest means of permanent prosperity; while the contrary course, in rulers or people, is dishonorable and ruinous.

title: I Kings 2:4
text: Continue; more literally, establish; that is, continue to fulfil his promise, which was made conditional upon the obedience of David's successors on the throne.

title: I Kings 2:7
text: The compassion of parents, and their readiness to do good, especially to the distressed, are often owned of God in blessings on their children, by leading them to imitate the good examples of their parents, and thus to become partakers of their reward.

title: I Kings 2:9
text: With blood; put him to a violent death for his crimes.  David judged it proper, at the time when Shimei met him, to give him his oath that he would not put him to death; but he felt that for the good of his kindgom such conduct ought to be punished with death, and Solomon was free to treat him according to his deserts.

title: I Kings 2:10
text: The city of David; Zion.   II Samuel 5:7

title: I Kings 2:15
text:
The kingdom was mine; his meaning was, that it belonged to him as David's oldest living son.  His second son Chileab,  II Samuel 3:3 , seems to have been already dead. 
 
God in his providence raises up one and puts down another; and when he has determined to elevate an individual to great power and influence, no efforts of men, however wisely directed or diligently pursued, will prevent it.

title: I Kings 2:19
text: No elevation of wise children will prevent them from loving and honoring aged parents, and as far as may be consistent with duty, complying with their requests.

title: I Kings 2:22
text:
Ask for him the kingdom; by this Solomon intimated to his mother, that, considering the relation Abishag had sustained to David, Adonijah's request for her implied an assertion of his right to the kingdom; for this was, according to the custom of those days, the way in which an usurper proceeded in respect to the concubines of his predecessor. 
 
No filal respect or affection, and no promises or engagements, should ever lead men to do what is morally wrong.

title: I Kings 2:23
text: God do so to me; put me to death, if I do not put Adonijah to death.

title: I Kings 2:24
text: Made me a house; secured him a posterity to inherit the throne after him.

title: I Kings 2:26
text:
Anathoth; a city in Benjamin. 
 
No elevation or official sanctity should be permitted to cover the guilt of crime, nor should the openly criminal or vicious be continued in any public employment.

title: I Kings 2:27
text: Abiathar, who was of the house of Eli, in the line of Ithamar, had been the high-priest after the death of Ahimelech his father.  Zadok, who succeeded him as high-priest, was descended from Aaron by the line of Eleazar.   I Chronicles 24:3

title: I Kings 2:28
text: Fled unto the tabernacle--the altar; as a place of safety.  See note to  I Kings 1:51 .

title: I Kings 2:31
text: Do as he hath said; slay him at the altar.  Solomon put substantial justice above the observance of an ancient usage.

title: I Kings 2:33
text: Shall there be peace; by putting Joab to death, they would be free from the guilt of conniving at the murders he had committed.  Genesis 9:6

title: I Kings 2:39
text: By a too eager desire that others should serve them, men may occasion their own ruin.

title: I Kings 2:42
text: Goest out; away from Jerusalem.

title: I Kings 3:2
text:
Only the people sacrificed; the word "only" implies that in general the people were obedient to the law of Moses, but that in this respect they did not comply it. 
 
  In high places; the high places where the people sacrificed, as here, to Jehovah, must be distinguished from the high places devoted to the worship of idols.  The law of Moses required that all offerings should be made at the tabernacle,  Leviticus 17:5 ; but previously to the building of the temple this rule was not strictly observed, even by such eminent prophets as Samuel,  I Samuel 9:12-14 .

title: I Kings 3:3
text: To love God is the highest duty, the greatest honor, and the supreme blessedness of men.  Those who do it, whatever their condition in this world, are kings and priests unto God, and will reign with him for ever and ever.

title: I Kings 3:5
text:
A dream; before men had the Bible to guide them, God sometimes made known to them his will in dreams. 
 
The fact that before the canon of Scripture was complete, God sometimes made known his will in dreams, gives no countenance to the idea that he continues to do it, or that any can safely be guided by dreams now.

title: I Kings 3:6
text: God in not only permitting, but inviting all in every condition who lack wisdom to ask it of him in faith and love, expecting on the ground of his promise to receive it, shows marvellous condescension and kindness; and if any to whom his is revealed do not become wise unto salvation, it will be their own fault.   James 1:5

title: I Kings 3:7
text:
A little child; young and inexperienced. 
 
  Go out or come in; act as ruler in Israel. 
 
A deep sense of want and a grateful recognition of the goodness of God, confidence in his willingness and power to help, and a disposition to ask of him, are a good preparation for receiving what we need.

title: I Kings 3:10
text: God is pleased when men from the heart ask for wisdom to understand and do their duty; and in all such cases he will give them not only what they ask, but numerous other blessings for this world and the world to come.

title: I Kings 3:11
text: Discern judgment; judge rightly in cases that might come before him.

title: I Kings 3:14
text:
Lengthen thy days; this and other promises made to Solomon were on condition that he should continue to obey God.   I Kings 6:12  
 
Obedience to God is conducive to health, long life, and the greatest enjoyment of temporal favors.  It is also conducive to the greatest usefulness, and is, through divine grace, a sure preparation for heaven.

title: I Kings 3:22
text: Persons who steal will also lie, and the practice of these sins prepares the heart for, and often leads to the commission of murder.

title: I Kings 3:23
text: An acquaintance with human nature, and with the working of the various passions of the human heart, is an important qualification for a judge, and will in various ways aid him in eliciting evidence and coming to right decisions.

title: I Kings 3:26
text: A mother's love is great and in high degree self-denying, but the practice of iniquity tends to destroy it, and to sink the mind to such baseness as to wish to rob others of what it cannot itself enjoy.

title: I Kings 3:27
text: She is the mother; having shown for the child a mother's love.

title: I Kings 4:2
text: A wise and good ruler, in the appointment of officers to take part in the administration of his government, will be especially careful to select such as are distinguished for wisdom and fidelity, and whose example and influence will be salutary to the people.

title: I Kings 4:21
text:
The river; Euphrates. 
 
Jehovah is a God of truth: when the word hath gone out of his mouth it standeth for ever; and though the fulfilment of his promises may be long delayed, in due time they will be accomplished.   Genesis 15:18

title: I Kings 4:22
text:
Provision; for all his numerous household and the dependents of his palace. 
 
  Thirty measures; in the Hebrew, thirty cors.  The cor was ten ephahs.  Reckoning the ephah at one bushel and one twelfth, a cor would be a little less than eleven bushels.

title: I Kings 4:24
text:
This side the river; the west side. 
 
  Tiphsah; a city on the Euphrates. 
 
  Azzah; Gaza; on the south-west of Canaan towards Egypt.

title: I Kings 4:25
text: The true glory of rulers is not the extent of their conquests, nor the splendor of their establishments, but the happiness and prosperity of their people.

title: I Kings 4:26
text: Forty thousand stalls of horses; Solomon had "a thousand and four hundred chariots,"  II Chronicles 1:14 , for which four thousand stalls would be a suitable proportion, according to the number given in  II Chronicles 9:25 .  It has been the opinion of some expositors from ancient times that this latter number was the original reading.

title: I Kings 4:28
text:
Dromedaries; a species of camels, remarkable for speed; but others understand the original word of a breed of swift horses. 
 
  The place where the officers were; the words, "the officers," were applied by the translators.  We might better render, either the place where they--the horses and dromedaries--were; or, the place where Solomon was.

title: I Kings 4:29
text: Jehovah has infinite fulness, and he can so replenish the minds and hearts of his people with knowledge, wisdom, and grace, that they will shine as lights in the world, and pour forth the richest blessings on all generations, to the end of time.

title: I Kings 4:33
text: All the works of God manifest his infinite power, wisdom, and goodness, and may suitably engage a measure of the thoughts and investigations of the wisest among men.

title: I Kings 5:1
text:
Tyre; a city of the Phenicians on the Mediterranean, north of Canaan. 
 
Kings as well as subjects are bound to love one another, to rejoice in each other's prosperity, and seek each other's good.

title: I Kings 5:4
text: Peace is the gift of God.  It should be received with gratitude, and employed by rulers and people in the prosecution of such works, and such only, as will be for his glory and their highest prosperity.

title: I Kings 5:6
text:
They; the subjects of Hiram. 
 
  Zidonians; inhabitants of Zidon, a city north of Tyre.

title: I Kings 5:9
text: The difference in the climate, soil, and productions of different countries, renders an interchange of commodities a mutual benefit; and this should ever be so conducted as to benefit all concerned.

title: I Kings 5:11
text: Twenty thousand measures; in the Hebrew, twenty thousand cors, and so also below, thirty thousand men consisted of Israelites.

title: I Kings 5:13
text:
Levy out of all Israel; this levy of thirty thousand men consisted of Israelites. 
 
The building of suitable houses for public worship is essential to the highest prosperity of the community, and all should be disposed to do their part towards the accomplishments.

title: I Kings 5:15
text:
Threescore and ten thousand--fourscore thousand; these one hundred and fifty thousand men were of the remnants of the Canaanites,  I Kings 9:20 II Chronicles 2:17-18 .  It should be borne in mind, 
 
(1) that every piece of timber had to be carried chiefly, if not entirely by hand, from Lebanon to the sea; 
 
(2) that these hewers and bearers prepared and collected timber not only for the temple, but also for Solomon's own house, and for many other sumptuous edifices which he was engaged in building. 
 
See  I Kings 9:15-23 .  It is reasonable to suppose that a portion of them were employed in hewing and transporting stones also, as well as timber.

title: I Kings 5:16
text: Three thousand and three hundred; the number of chief officers set over the one hundred and fifty thousand men is here stated at three thousand three hundred; while in  I Kings 9:23 , the chief officers over Solomon's work are given as five hundred and fifty.  The sum of these two numbers is three thousand eight hundred and fifty.  In  II Chronicles 2:17 , the chief officers set over the one hundred and fifty thousand are stated at three thousand six hundred; while in  II Chronicles 8:10 , the chief officers that bare rule over the people are given as two hundred and fifty.  These two numbers again make three thousand eight hundred and fifty.  It is evident that the apparent discrepancy between the two accounts, in Kings and Chronicles, arises simply from different modes of classifying these officers.

title: I Kings 5:18
text: Stone-squarers; in the margin, Giblites; inhabitants of Gebal a town near Zidon.   Joshua 13:5 Ezekiel 27:9

title: I Kings 6:1
text:
Zif; the second month of their ecclesiastical year, answering to a part of April and May. 
 
The successful accomplishment of a great and difficult undertaking depends much on the proper preparation for it; and the time, money, and labor so spent are as needful and as useful as those spent in any part of the work.

title: I Kings 6:2
text: Threescore cubits--twenty cubits; the proportion of the length of the temple to its breadth was the same as that of the tabernacle; but each dimension was twice as great.

title: I Kings 6:4
text: Windows of narrow lights; or, windows with fixed lattices.

title: I Kings 6:5
text: The oracle; the inner apartment of the temple, twenty cubits square, situated at its west end, and answering to the "holy of holies" in the tabernacle.  The chambers were thus built around the house on its two sides and end, the front, which was towards the east, remaining open.

title: I Kings 6:6
text:
The nethermost chamber; here put collectively for the whole lower range of chambers, of which there were three stories. 
 
  Five cubits--six cubits--seven cubits; the walls of the temple were thickest at the bottom, with offsets on the outside, making horizontal ledges a cubit in width.  On these ledges the timbers of the chambers rested on the side towards the temple.  Thus the necessity of letting them into the wall was avoided. 
 
  Narrowed rests; the ledges produced by diminishing the thickness of the wall on the outside.

title: I Kings 6:8
text:
For the middle chamber; the middle chamber of the lower story on the south side.  There seems to have been but one entrance to the chambers. 
 
  Unto the middle chamber; the middle chamber of the second story.

title: I Kings 6:10
text: And then he built; the word "then" is not in the original, and obscures the sense.  We might better render, "And he built the chambers," etc.  He goes on to describe their height, which was five cubits, apparently for each story, making fifteen cubits in all.  This would leave ample room for the windows of the temple above them.

title: I Kings 6:12
text: However much may be expended in building and ornamenting houses for the worship of God, none of the worshippers will be accepted but those who worship him in spirit and in truth.

title: I Kings 6:16
text: On the sides; more exactly, in the hindermost part.  He is describing the holy of holies.

title: I Kings 6:17
text: Before it; before the most holy place.

title: I Kings 6:18
text:
Knops; or, gourds; that is, ornamental figures resembling gourds. 
 
  There was no stone seen; the walls of the temple were of hewn stone; but these were entirely covered with cedar planks.

title: I Kings 6:19
text: Although Jehovah dwells not in temples made with hands, yet he is peculiarly present where his people assemble to acknowledge, adore, and praise him; and there, by the proclamation of his truth, he will communicate to them a knowledge of his will.

title: I Kings 6:20
text: The altar; the altar of frankincense, which stood just outside of the partition which separated the most holy from the holy place.

title: I Kings 6:21
text: Partition by the chains of gold; or, a partition of chains of gold, to divide the holy from the most holy place.

title: I Kings 6:27
text: He set the cherubim; they were not arrnged face to face, like those upon the mercy-seat, but side by side, with their backs to the farthest or western side of the oracle; so that their outspread wings extended throughout its whole breadth.

title: I Kings 6:30
text: Gold, although among the most precious things of earth, is nevertheless worthless and fit only to be trodden under foot, compared with that holiness of heart and life without which no man can see the Lord.

title: I Kings 6:33
text: The door of the temple; the door leading from the porch into the holy place.

title: I Kings 6:36
text: The inner court; directly before the porch, in which was the altar of burnt-offering.

title: I Kings 6:37
text:
In the fourth year; of Solomon's reign. 
 
That which is undertaken in the fear and love of God, and is prosecuted according to his will, may be expected in due time to be successfully and joyfully accomplished.

title: I Kings 6:38
text: The eighth month; answering to a part of October and November.

title: I Kings 7:1
text: While convenient and comfortable dwellings are blessings for which men should be grateful, their great concern should be to secure a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

title: I Kings 7:2
text:
He built also the house; literally, And he built the house, etc. It is probable that  I Kings 6:1  refers to the structure of Solomon's house as a whole, consisting of several divisions; while the particular description of the parts begins with  I Kings 6:2 , thus: And he finished all his house; and [as a part of it] he built the house of the forest of Lebanon, etc.  This seems to have been in Jerusalem, and to have been so called from the multitude of cedar pillars and timbers employed in making it. 
 
  Upon four rows of cedar pillars; in accordance with the general style of oriental palaces, it is probable that it was constructed without of massive hewn stones,  I Kings 7:9-11 , and resting within on rows of cedar pillars, which were four in number, arranged around the four sides of a hollow oblong area.

title: I Kings 7:3
text: Beams; the Hebrew word here used is elsewhere rendered chambers,  I Kings 6:5-6 , and this seems to be the preferable rendering here.  We may then render the whole verse thus: And it was covered with cedar above upon the chambers which lay on the pillars--forty and five [chambers,] fifteen to a row.  We may understand the rows of chambers, as successive stories of fifteen chambers each built round the open area.

title: I Kings 7:4
text:
In three years; that is, according to the above interpretation, three rows, one for each story. 
 
  Light was against light; either the lights of the middle story were directly above those of the lower, and so of the third; or the lights on one side of the area were directly opposite to those of the other side.

title: I Kings 7:5
text: Square, with the windows; or, were squared with beams; covered above with straight beams, so as to make a square and not a vaulted opening.

title: I Kings 7:6
text:
A porch of pillars; generally supposed to have been in front of the structure just described. 
 
  And the porch--were before them; or, and [another] porch was before them, [the pillars of the porch of pillars,] and pillars and a threshold before them.

title: I Kings 7:8
text: The more husbands and wives are united in their views, judgments, and efforts, dwelling together as heirs of the grace of life, the more happy they will be, and the more useful to all who may feel their influence.

title: I Kings 7:9
text: All these; all these several structures that have been described.

title: I Kings 7:12
text:
The great court round about; plainly enclosing all the various structures above described, which, taken as a whole, seem to be what is meant by Solomon's house,  I Kings 7:1 . 
 
  Both for the inner court--and for the porch; or, even according to the inner court--and according to the porch.

title: I Kings 7:14
text:
Brass; this term was applied to various metals, composed chiefly or wholly of copper. 
 
All natural endowments, as well as all spiritual graces, come from God. He bestows them in different measures upon different individuals, and in his service requires of each according to that he hath, and not according to that he hath not.

title: I Kings 7:16
text: Chapiters; capitals or heads of the columns.  They had a swell in their central part called "the belly,"  I Kings 7:20 , which was surrounded with checker-work and chain-work,  I Kings 7:17 , with two rows of pomegrantes around each, besides an ornament of lily-work,  I Kings 7:19 I Kings 7:22 .

title: I Kings 7:21
text:
Jachin; meaning, he shall establish, or make it stand. 
 
  Boaz; in strength.

title: I Kings 7:23
text:
Molten sea; a very large vat or basin for water. 
 
The method of divine worship prescribed under every dispensation, the preparations for it, the mode of conducting it, and the truths inculcated by it, have all tended to impress upon the worshippers a conviction of their moral pollution, and the necessity of spiritual purification in order to preparation for heaven.

title: I Kings 7:26
text: Two thousand baths; a bath is supposed to have been about seven and a half gallons.

title: I Kings 7:27
text: Bases; tables or platforms for the vessels of water to stand on. These bases were complicated in their structure and highly ornamented, so that it is difficult to obtain, from the description here given, any thing more than a general idea of their form and parts.

title: I Kings 7:28
text:
Borders; the word in the original seems to mean pannels, on the four sides, that were ornamented with figures of lions, oxen, and cherubs. 
 
  Ledges; raised work around the edges of the borders.

title: I Kings 7:29
text: Certain additions made of thin work; the original seems to mean, festoons of flowers hanging down.

title: I Kings 7:30
text: Undersetters; literally, shoulders, that is, projections.

title: I Kings 7:31
text:
The mouth of it; of the laver.  The mouth of the laver seems here, from its position, to be the lower part of the laver, through which its waters were discharged. 
 
  The chapiter; the head of the base above described.

title: I Kings 7:46
text: Succoth and Zarthan; places near the Jordan, and not far from Jericho.

title: I Kings 7:48
text: In order to the right use of wealth, all persons need and should habitually seek wisdom from above.  How much, or what proportion, is to be employed in one way, and what in another, in order most to honor God and do good, he has not definitely prescribed.  But each one should endeavor so to act as a steward of God, that when called to give up his account, he may do it with joy, and not with grief.

title: I Kings 8:1
text:
Bring up the ark; from mount Zion in the south-west part of Jerusalem, where David lived, to the temple on mount Moriah, an elevation in the east part of the city. 
 
The most costly and splendid temple without the presence and favor of God, is but a dead mass of useless matter; and the most exact and gorgeous forms of worship, without love and faith in the worshippers, are no more pleasing to him than sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.  I Corinthians 13:1

title: I Kings 8:2
text:
The feast; of tabernacles. 
 
  Ethanim; answering to a part of September and October.

title: I Kings 8:4
text: The tabernacle of the congregation; as this was the peculiar name by which the tabernacle constructed by Moses in the wilderness was known, it is probable that it had been brought from Gibeon, where it was at the beginning of Solomon's reign-- I Chronicles 16:39 I Chronicles 21:29 --to be deposited in the temple.  Some, however, suppose that we are here to understand the tabernacle which David had prepared for the ark when he brought it from the house of Obed-edom.   II Samuel 6:17

title: I Kings 8:6
text: Under the wings of the cheribum; the two cherubim of olive-wood that Solomon had placed in the holy of holies,  I Kings 6:23-28 .

title: I Kings 8:8
text:
The staves; those by which the ark was borne,  Exodus 25:13-15 . They were drawn partly out, so that their ends projected into the holy place. 
 
  Unto this day; an expression which the author of the books of Kings seems to have retained from "the book of the acts of Solomon."  I Kings 11:41

title: I Kings 8:10
text:
The cloud; the symbol of God's presence,  Exodus 19:16 Exodus 20:21   Exodus 40:34-35 Isaiah 6:4 Revelation of John 15:8 . 
 
When the people of God have dedicated to him a house, and assemble in it to worship him in spirit and in truth, they may expect glorious manifestations of his presence, and rich spiritual joys.

title: I Kings 8:17
text: To every sincere desire for the promotion of his glory and the good of men, God is witness; and whether it can consistently be now granted or not, he will connect it with great results, and bestow upon it gracious and glorious reward.

title: I Kings 8:22
text:
Stood before the altar; he presented himself before the altar, standing with his face towards the congregation, and then kneeled down and spread out his hands as he prayed,  I Kings 8:54 . 
 
Every ruler should be a man of prayer, and on suitable occasions should publicly set the example of acknowledging and adoring God; blessing him for his goodness, and seeking of him those mercies which are needed for rulers and people.

title: I Kings 8:26
text: Verified; shown to be true, by its fulfilment.

title: I Kings 8:29
text:
May be open; look with favor. 
 
  Toward; in  I Kings 8:33 .

title: I Kings 8:31
text: An oath be laid upon him; this oath he was required to take before the altar.

title: I Kings 8:33
text:
In; toward,  I Kings 8:30 .  The word in the original means in, or toward, according to the connection. 
 
The public calamities of a people are caused by their sins; and repentance, reformation, and earnest supplications to God are his appointed means for their removal.

title: I Kings 8:38
text: The plague of his own heart; the sorrow that is his own special burden, and which he feels to be the chastisement from God for his sin.

title: I Kings 8:41
text:
For thy names's sake; on account of what he had heard about God, and for the purpose of worshipping him and sharing in the blessings of his people. 
 
All enlightened and sincere friends of God earnestly desire that the blessings which he bestows on them may be enjoyed by all people, and that for this end he may be revealed to them and they may be taught to worship him in the beauty of holiness.

title: I Kings 8:46
text: There is no land so distant or dark, and no condition so trying, that men may not think of their sins as the cause of their sorrows, repent of them, from the heart make supplication to God, and in due time receive abundant answers to their prayers.

title: I Kings 8:58
text: God is the author of the inclination to love and serve him, and no greater blessing is ever bestowed by him on earth, than a disposition to believe his declarations and keep his commandments.

title: I Kings 8:63
text: A sacrifice of peace-offerings--two and twenty thousand oxen-- twenty thousand sheep; certain prescribed portions of these peace-offerings were burned,  Leviticus 3:3-4 Leviticus 3:10-11 , and from the rest he furnished a feast for the immense multitude of the people assembled from all parts of the land for fourteen days,  I Kings 8:65-66 .  In this he imitated the example of David when he removed the ark to Zion,  II Samuel 6:17 II Samuel 6:19 .  Thus was strikingly typified the spiritual feast which a greater than Solomon has provided for all who believe, by the sacrifice of his blood,  Isaiah 25:6 .

title: I Kings 8:65
text:
The entering in of Hamath; on the north border of Canaan. 
 
Sincere and upright worship of God, and hearty obedience to his commands, is a source of gladness and exceeding joy.  It raises the soul to the highest enjoyment which can be found on earth, and fits it for perfect and endless bliss in heaven.

title: I Kings 9:3
text:
Hallowed; accepted their consecration of the temple to his service. 
 
All sincere and hearty supplications to God will be accepted, and all offerings presented in love to him receive a gracious reward.

title: I Kings 9:6
text: Continued obedience to God is needful in order to the continuance of his favors; and if those who have been distinguished by his mercies rebel against him, they will be distinguished in their punishment.

title: I Kings 9:8
text: Which is high; its height shall only make it a more conspicuous object of reproach.

title: I Kings 9:12
text: Different men have different tastes, which lead them to follow different occupations and live in different places.  Some are attracted by the noise and bustle of cities, others by the stillness and quiet of the country, and both may be where God calls them, and be mutually serviceable to each other.

title: I Kings 9:13
text: Cabul; the meaning of this word cannot be certainly determined, but it evidently denotes something displeasing.

title: I Kings 9:15
text:
Levy; levy of men,  I Kings 9:21 I Kings 5:15 . 
 
  Millo; a part of the citidel or fortifications of Jerusalem. 
 
  Hazor; in Naphtali. 
 
  Megiddo; in Issachar. 
 
  Gezer; in Ephraim.

title: I Kings 9:17
text:
Beth-horon; in the tribe of Benjamin. 
 
  Nether; lower.  There were two places of this name, the upper and the lower, with a steep descent between,  Joshua 10:11 Joshua 16:3 .

title: I Kings 9:18
text:
Baalath; in the territory of Dan. 
 
  Tadmor; supposed still to be seen in the desert east of Damascus. 
 
The most opulent cities, and the most splendid human works, are liable to become a heap of ruins.  None should therefore set their hearts on them, but all should secure durable riches and righteousness, treasures in the heavens which will never pass away.

title: I Kings 9:25
text: All who are distinguished by wealth, power, and influence, should also be distinguished for habitual devotion to God, and regular, conscientious attendance upon his worship.

title: I Kings 9:26
text:
Ezion-geber; near the north end of the east branch of the Red sea. 
 
As commerce is a source of wealth, and seamen are exposed to numerous privations, hardships, dangers, and vices, those who are benefited by their services should, in addition to giving them suitable compensation and temporal comforts, furnish them with the Bible and other good books, and as far as practicable with all the means of grace.

title: I Kings 9:28
text: Ophir; supposed to be some place either in Arabia, or on the Indian ocean.

title: I Kings 10:1
text:
Sheba; supposed to have been a country in the southern part of Arabia near the south end of the Red sea. 
 
  Heard of the fame; probably by the ships that went down from Ezion-geber. 
 
  Prove him; ascertain whether he was as wise as he had been represented to be. 
 
The highest honor and the noblest fame is that which relates to the name of Jehovah, and the greatest wisdom consists in learning and doing his will.   Psalms 111:10

title: I Kings 10:3
text: The richest and most profitable knowledge that can be communicated, is the knowledge of God and the way of acceptably worshipping him.

title: I Kings 10:5
text: No more spirit; she was utterly astonished.

title: I Kings 10:7
text: The blessings which God bestows upon those who love and obey him exceed all human description, and they never can be fully known except by those who receive and enjoy them.

title: I Kings 10:9
text: Wise and good rulers are manifestations of God's peculiar favor to a people, while foolish and wicked ones are tokens of his wrath.

title: I Kings 10:11
text: Almug-trees; according to some a species of sandalwood, fine-grained and fragrant, much employed in the East at the present day for elegant articles of cabinet-work.

title: I Kings 10:14
text: Six hundred threescore and six talents of gold; a talent consisted of three thousand shekels.  The shekel of silver has been variously estimated at from fifty to sixty cents.  This would make the talent of silver from one thousand five hundred to one thousand eight hundred dollars.  The talent of gold was many times greater, according to the relative value of gold to that of silver.

title: I Kings 10:17
text: Three pounds; in the Hebrew, three manehs, the maneh being generally reckoned at one hundred shekels.

title: I Kings 10:18
text: A great increase of wealth is liable to be abused, and instead of leading men to God, to be prostituted to purposes of personal aggrandizement, external pomp, magnificence, and show.

title: I Kings 10:21
text: It was nothing accounted of; that is, silver, from its abundance.

title: I Kings 10:22
text: Navy of Tarshish; some have understood the words, "navy of Tarshish," to mean a navy of ships of a peculiar construction called Tarshish ships, though they might sail to other ports, just as the English word Indiaman is used.  Others suppose that Solomon and Hiram had two navies, one on the Mediterranean, which went to Tarshish in Spain, the other at Ezion-geber on the eastern arm of the Red sea, which went to Ophir.  In the voyage to Tarshish, "ivory, apes, and peacocks," could be easily obtained from the northern coast of Africa. Silver was very abundant in Tarshish.  This may explain its abundance in Jerusalem in Solomon's day.

title: I Kings 10:24
text:
All the earth; people from all surrounding nations. 
 
The possession of peculiar wisdom lays men under peculiar obligations to glorify God by instructing their fellow men, and promoting their highest welfare.

title: I Kings 11:1
text:
Strange women; women of foreign nations. 
 
The union for life of one man with one woman, according to the appointment of God, is essential to the highest excellence, usefulness, and happiness in life; and the neglect or violation of the original institution of marriage is a source of many of the most direful evils to which men on the earth are exposed.

title: I Kings 11:2
text: However great the blessings which any one may have enjoyed, and however well he may in times past have improved them, yet, if left to himself, he is liable to depart from God, and to fall into the most abominable transgressions.

title: I Kings 11:4
text: Licentiousness weakens the understanding, corrupts the affections, stupefies the conscience, hardens the heart, and debases all the powers of the human soul.  No talents, acquisitions, or renown, can keep the soul which is under its power from the practice of the most degrading and destructive sins.

title: I Kings 11:5
text:
Milcom; supposed to be the same as Molech.   I Kings 11:7 . 
 
  Abomination; idol-god.

title: I Kings 11:9
